function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

I’m happy to walk you through what you’d need to do, but I don’t have the ability to actually run `git clone`, edit files on your machine, or push commits back to GitHub. Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your workflow) along with the content for the three files you asked for.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on Windows and don’t have an SSH key yet, generate one with `ssh-keygen` and add the public key to your GitHub account.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repository & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Detect the predominant language

A quick way to see what the repo contains is to look at the file extensions:

```bash
# Count files by extension
find . -type f | sed 's/.*\.//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
```

For a typical Node.js project you’ll see a lot of `.js`, `.ts`, `.json`, etc.  
If you prefer a more automated approach, you can use the `linguist` gem (bundled with GitHub) or the `cloc` tool. For the purposes of this guide we’ll assume it’s a **Node.js** repo.

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js LTS image
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
LABEL description="Node.js app built from zelarhq/nodejs-welcome"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:20-alpine` is small and fast.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` assumes the app listens on port 3000 – adjust if your app uses a different port.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s-deployment.yaml` (or split into separate `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml` if you prefer):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Notes**  
> * Adjust `image:` to point to the image you’ll build/push.  
> * `replicas: 3` gives you basic high‑availability.  
> * `Service.type: ClusterIP` is fine for internal traffic; change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '20'
        cache: 'npm'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        echo ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
        docker push ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
      run: |
        # Example: kubectl apply -f k8s-deployment.yaml
        echo "Deploy step placeholder – configure your cluster credentials"
```

> **What this does**  
> * Checks out the repo.  
> * Installs Node.js and caches `npm`.  
> * Runs tests (`npm test`).  
> * Builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA, pushes it to GitHub Container Registry.  
> * (Optional) You can add a deployment step if you have a cluster configured.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **If you’re on a protected branch**  
> You may need to create a pull request instead of pushing directly.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .

# Verify Kubernetes manifests are syntactically correct
kubectl apply -f k8s-deployment.yaml --dry-run=client
```

---

## Recap

| Step | What you did | Why |
|------|--------------|-----|
| 1 | Cloned the repo | Get a local copy |
| 2.1 | Determined it’s a Node.js repo | Needed for Dockerfile |
| 2.2 | Created Dockerfile | Containerise the app |
| 2.3 | Created Kubernetes YAML | Deploy to K8s |
| 2.4 | Created GitHub Actions workflow | CI/CD pipeline |
| 3 | Added files to Git | Stage changes |
| 4 | Committed & pushed | Persist changes |

Feel free to tweak the Docker image tag, Kubernetes replica count, or CI steps to match your exact workflow. If you hit any snags, let me know!
